list.listitem: Clinical symptoms depend on type of mercury exposure (elemental, inorganic, or organic); pulmonary, CNS, or renal systems are most likely to be affected by mercury poisoning. C
Chelation therapy is indicated in severe cases of mercury toxicity. C

Although no consistent association has been shown between thimerosal-containing vaccines and neurodevelopmental outcomes, B thimerosal has been removed from all pediatric vaccines with the exception of a few types of influenza vaccine.
Children with amalgam dental fillings have not been shown to score worse on cognitive assessments than children with resin composite, although urine mercury levels are increased. B

Pregnant women, women who may become pregnant, nursing mothers, and children should avoid consumption of shark, swordfish, golden bass, king mackerel, and tilefish because of concerns about high mercury levels in these fishes. C
Source: thermometers, sphygmomanometers, incandescent lights, dental amalgam, batteries, paints, gold and silver smelting, and as a contaminant in foods and cosmetics

Effects: (1) hazardous in vaporized state, (2) pulmonary effects including acute respiratory distress syndrome in severe cases, (3) long-term vapor inhalation can lead to CNS effects, (4) not well absorbed by GI tract (<0.1% absorbed)
There is mixed evidence regarding the effect of mercury exposure on blood pressure.
An association between mercury and autism spectrum disorder has been reported in a systematic review of 44 studies.
Excretion: primarily fecal
Source: teething powders, skin creams, disinfectants, production of vinyl chloride
Effects: (1) GI ulceration and acute hemorrhage, (2) nephrotoxic (including acute tubular necrosis), (3) neurotoxic
Excretion: primarily fecal
Source: industrial compounds (pesticides), consumption of fish (90%-100% absorbed from GI tract), thimerosal
Effects: toxic to CNS (crosses placenta, therefore, toxic to fetal cerebral cortex)
Excretion: primarily fecal
Many mercury compounds no longer sold in the US
Organic mercury fungicides no longer licensed for commercial use
Electronic equipment has replaced mercury containing thermometers and sphygmomanometers
With the exception of some influenza vaccines, none of the vaccines used in children contains thimerosal as a preservative.
In the event of a mercury spill, a spill kit is recommended, or contact environmental health agencies for assistance.

Pregnant women and women of childbearing age should avoid consumption of tilefish, swordfish, mackerel, and shark; other individuals should limit consumption of these fish to 1 serving per week; consumption of other types of fish and shellfish should be limited to 2 servings per week. Special caution with Great Lakes fish: none if pregnant and no more than once per week otherwise.
Obtain thorough history of nature and duration of symptoms (particularly neurologic)
Nature of exposure (inhalation, consumption, dermatologic)
Obtain objective proof, if possible, of the ingested product and the quantity

If exposure not readily apparent, obtain information about: (1) occupation; (2) quantity, frequency, and type of seafood consumption; (3) potential chemical exposures (vapors, paints); (4) hobbies; (5) types of cosmetics used
Neurologic: including vision, memory testing, assess for tremor, and cerebellar examination
Pulmonary: thorough auscultation
GI: assessing for excessive salivation, severity of abdominal pain, rectal examination with stool testing for occult blood
Dermatologic: erythematous or desquamating skin, grayish discoloration of mucous membranes
Psychiatric: anxiety, irritability, memory loss, fatigue
Acrodynia (pink disease) in the pediatric population, a result of excess mercury exposure, consists of body rash, swelling of palms and feet, skin desquamation, irritability, fever and sweating
Urine: 24-hour urine collection for urinary mercury concentration (normal <10-20 mcg/L); does not necessarily correlate with chronicity or severity of toxic effects
Blood: normal values <10 mcg/L

Hair: concentrations in hair generally do not exceed 10 mg/kg, but with a high rate of false-positive results, hair analysis should not be used alone to confirm mercury exposure or toxicity. A systematic review has concluded that the lowest observable adverse effect hair concentration (LOAEHC) should be 0.3 microg/g of maternal hair mercury
CBC, renal lytes (to monitor for potential GI hemorrhage or renal involvement)
Imaging: plain radiographs (elemental mercury is radiopaque)
Address the ABCs (airway, breathing, circulation). Do not give ipecac or activated charcoal without recommendation from a poison center or emergency department
Mercury inhalation: supportive care and possibly extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO).
Mercury ingestion: activated charcoal can be used but does not bind mercury well; consider gastric lavage for organic form of ingestion
Dermatologic exposure: remove clothing; copious irrigation

Indications for chelation therapy are not clearly established; It is usually reserved for those patients with laboratory evidence or symptoms of severe poisoning. Specific agents are summarized below:
Succimer (DMSA): oral formulation. There is only limited evidence of efficacy
Dimercaprol: IM injection
D-penicillamine: excreted in urine; therefore, not used in renal failure
DMPS: not approved by Food and Drug Administration and not widely available in the US
N-acetylcysteine: may be effective in methyl-mercury poisoning
Hemodialysis may be necessary in severe toxicity when renal failure is present
Neostigmine may help motor function in methylmercury toxicity, as this form often leads to acetylcholine deficiency
Monitor symptoms and urine/blood levels
Ensure removal of mercury exposure/source
Progressive neurologic and renal deterioration with continued exposure
Severe exposure left untreated can result in fatality
Mild exposures can result in complete recovery.
More severe cases can have residual neurologic and pulmonary problems despite therapeutic intervention.
